questions.q: What is the fragile base class problem?
questions.explain: The parent's author refactors something that callers of the parent cannot notice, such as whether addItems calls addItem. A subclass that depended on that detail breaks without being touched.
options: A base class that throws too many errors
A subclass breaks when its parent changes internally, even though the parent's own behaviour stays correct
A base class that cannot be extended because its fields are private
A class hierarchy that uses too much memory

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: PointsCart.addItems adds 3 points, then the parent's addItems calls this.addItem three times. this is the points cart, so the override runs and adds 3 more points.

questions.q: The subclass only overrides addItem. Then the parent is changed as shown. What does this print?
questions.explain: The new addItems pushes directly instead of calling addItem, so the override never runs for the bulk add. Only the single addItem("rice") earns a point.

questions.q: Which of these does a subclass not get from extends?
questions.explain: Private fields belong to the class body that declares them; even a subclass cannot read them. The other three are exactly what makes subclasses coupled to their parents.
options: The parent's method code running with this set to the subclass instance
Calls from inside the parent's methods to this.method() reaching the subclass's overrides

questions.q: A ReadOnlyAccount extends Account overrides deposit() to throw. Why is this a poor use of inheritance?
questions.explain: The Liskov substitution principle: a subclass must keep the promises its parent makes to callers. Sounding like "a kind of account" in English is not enough.
options: Because extends cannot override methods that change state
Code that works with any Account and calls deposit breaks when handed a ReadOnlyAccount, even though instanceof Account is true
Because throwing inside a method is not allowed in classes
Because the subclass uses more memory than the parent

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The wrapper calls addItems on the cart it holds. Inside the cart, this.addItem is the cart's own method, never the wrapper's, so points are counted once.
options: TypeError: cart.addItems is not a function

questions.q: What is the main cost of a forwarding wrapper compared with a subclass?
questions.explain: Methods you do not forward do not exist on the wrapper. That is extra typing, and often a benefit: the wrapper chooses its own public interface.
options: You must write a forwarding method for every method you want the wrapper to offer
It is always slower than inheritance by a large factor

questions.q: Two wrappers around the same gateway. What does this print?
questions.explain: The outer wrapper runs first. withVat(withFee(base)): 100 × 2 = 200, then + 10 = 210. withFee(withVat(base)): 100 + 10 = 110, then × 2 = 220. The order of wrapping is a real decision.

questions.q: What makes a wrapper a decorator in the sense used in the lesson?
questions.explain: Same shape in, same shape out. That is why withRetry(withLogging(gateway)) works: each layer looks like a gateway to the next.
options: It extends the class it wraps
It offers the same methods as the object it wraps, so callers cannot tell them apart and wrappers can be stacked
It is written as an arrow function

questions.q: A withRetry wrapper retries a payment after a network timeout. What must be true for this to be safe?
questions.explain: A timeout means "no answer", not "no payment". Without idempotency by reference, a retry can charge the customer twice.
options: The retry must wait at least one second
The provider must treat the retry as the same payment (for example by its reference), because the timed-out attempt may actually have succeeded
The wrapper must extend the gateway class

questions.q: A checkout holds a delivery object and calls delivery.feeKobo(order). Which statement is correct?
questions.explain: This is delegation to a strategy. The checkout depends on an interface, "has feeKobo", not on any class. Relying on what an object can do is duck typing.
options: The checkout must know every delivery option in a switch
Any object with a feeKobo(order) method can be used, and it can be swapped at runtime or in tests
The strategy must be a class instance, not a plain object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ₦49,900 is below the ₦50,000 threshold, so the "free" strategy still charges ₦2,500. Both totals are ₦52,400.

questions.q: Where should a checkout check that its gateway has a charge method?
questions.explain: A missing method is a bug in how the program was assembled. Failing at construction surfaces it before the first customer tries to pay.
options: Inside every call to charge, just before it
Once, in the constructor, so a wiring mistake stops the program at start-up

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object.assign overwrites existing keys without a warning, so the mixin's describe replaces the class's own. That silent clash is the main risk of object mixins.

questions.q: After Object.assign(Order.prototype, Taggable), what does order instanceof Taggable do?
questions.explain: The right side of instanceof must be callable. Object mixins give you no identity to test; you can only check for the methods.
options: Throws a TypeError, because Taggable is a plain object, not a function

questions.q: A Describable mixin's method reads this.id. Which mixin risk is this?
questions.explain: Nothing states that users of the mixin must have an id. The mistake does not throw; it produces wrong output.
options: A hidden dependency: the requirement is not written anywhere, and objects without id quietly print undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The outermost mixin's method runs first and calls super. In A, Loud upper-cases what Polite returned, including ", please". In B, Polite adds ", please" after Loud has already upper-cased the clerk's text.
options:
NEXT CUSTOMER, please
NEXT CUSTOMER, PLEASE

NEXT CUSTOMER, PLEASE
NEXT CUSTOMER, please

NEXT CUSTOMER, PLEASE
NEXT CUSTOMER, PLEASE

questions.q: Why does the lesson say class-expression mixins are "still inheritance"?
questions.explain: SoftDeletable(Timestamped(Record)) builds a chain of anonymous classes. Every coupling problem of extends applies to it.
options: Each mixin becomes a real class in the prototype chain, so self-calls and overrides couple the layers exactly like ordinary subclasses

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Spread reads each property's value once. The product gets a plain data property holding 10; the getter is gone. Copy descriptors, or use methods, to keep live values.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Copying descriptors copies the getter function itself, so reading left still runs it and sees the current stock.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The object is frozen, and this file is a module (strict mode), so replacing a property throws a TypeError. The balance itself is a variable in the closure, not a property, so nothing outside could have reached it anyway: 500,000 − 120,000 = 380,000.

questions.q: When is a class a better choice than a factory function that returns an object full of closures?
questions.explain: Closures give each object its own functions. For a few thousand objects that is fine; for millions, sharing methods on a prototype saves memory.
options: When you create very many objects, because each factory object carries its own copies of the method functions while class instances share methods on the prototype
When the object has fewer than three methods

questions.q: The coupon should come off before VAT. What does this print?
questions.explain: Coupon first: (1,000,000 − 100,000) × 1.075 = 967,500. VAT first: 1,075,000 − 100,000 = 975,000. The order of the rule list is part of the business rule.

questions.q: In const coupon = (code, offKobo) => (amount, order) => …, what is coupon("WELCOME", 200000)?
questions.explain: A function that returns a function. The returned rule closes over code and offKobo, so one definition covers every coupon.
options: A rule function that remembers the code and the amount off, ready to be put in the rule list
An error, because arrow functions cannot return functions

questions.q: What happens when a subclass method reads this.#items, where #items is declared only in the parent class?
questions.explain: Private names are checked when the code is parsed. A subclass cannot even mention the parent's private fields, so it has to use the public API.
options: It works, because the subclass inherits the field
The file fails to load with a SyntaxError: the private name is not declared in an enclosing class
It throws a TypeError only when the method is called

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: instanceof only checks the prototype chain, which Object.create can fake. #number in value is a brand check: only objects built by the constructor have the private field.

questions.q: Why does wrapping a class instance with private fields in a Proxy often throw when you read a getter through it?
questions.explain: Private fields are attached to the real object, not to the proxy. An explicit forwarding wrapper calls methods on the real object, so it does not have this problem.
options: The getter runs with this set to the proxy, and the proxy object does not have the private field
Private fields are deleted when a proxy is created
Proxies only work on plain objects

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Static methods are inherited, and inside a static method this is the class it was called on. new this(owner) therefore builds a SavingsAccount.
options: TypeError: this is not a constructor

questions.q: When does the code in a class's static { … } block run?
questions.explain: A static block is class-wide set-up, run once. It suits things like building one shared Intl.NumberFormat for all instances.
options: Every time an instance is created
Once, when the class definition is evaluated
The first time a static method is called
Only if the class is exported

questions.q: A class has get totalKobo() and no setter. Code in an ES module runs cart.totalKobo = 0. What happens?
questions.explain: Modules and classes are strict mode, and assigning to an accessor with no setter throws in strict mode. The caller learns about the mistake immediately.
options: A TypeError: the property has only a getter
The getter is replaced by the number 0

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Private fields are invisible to JSON.stringify, and getters live on the prototype, so the cart serialises as {}. A toJSON method decides what the JSON looks like.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in a getter?
questions.explain: Reading a property should be cheap and change nothing. I/O and side effects belong in methods, preferably async ones, so callers can see them.
options: Loading the customer's orders from the database
Adding up the prices of the lines already in memory

questions.q: A cart keeps its lines in #lines. Why does its lines() method return this.#lines.map((l) => ({ ...l })) rather than this.#lines?
questions.explain: A private field protects the variable, not the object it points to. Handing out copies keeps the cart the only code that can change its lines.
options: Because map is faster than returning the array
Returning the internal array would let callers push into it or edit lines, bypassing the cart's checks and its lock
Because private fields cannot be returned from methods
To convert the lines to JSON

questions.q: A checkout reserves stock for each line, then charges the card. The charge fails. What should it do?
questions.explain: Keep a list of what you reserved and undo that list. If the second reservation fails, the first one must be released too.
options: Nothing; the stock will be corrected by the next stock count
Release exactly the reservations it made, then report the error
Release all stock for every product in the shop
Retry the charge until it succeeds

questions.q: Why is new Checkout({ gateway }) easier to test than a Checkout whose constructor runs this.gateway = new CardGateway()?
questions.explain: Passing collaborators in (dependency injection) is what makes them replaceable. A class that creates its own gateway can only be tested against that gateway.
options: A test can pass a fake gateway that fails on demand and records its calls, without touching a real payment provider
It is not easier; both are the same

questions.q: Which is the best candidate for extends?
questions.explain: Error is designed to be extended, callers rely on instanceof and catch, and a declined-payment error really can stand in for an error everywhere. The others are better as wrappers, strategies or separate types.
options: A LoggingCart that adds logging to a cart
A CheapDelivery that changes how the delivery fee is computed
A ReadOnlyCart that throws on every change

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: key in target follows the prototype chain, so the inherited Object.prototype.toString counts as a clash. total was copied before the loop reached toString, so it exists.

questions.q: Write a class CountingStock that wraps (does not extend) any stock object with set(sku, qty), restock(sku, qty) and level(sku). It forwards all three and counts how many times its own set and restock were called, in a getter changes. The program should print 2 15.
questions.explain: Because the wrapper calls methods on the stock it holds, Stock.restock's internal this.set stays inside the stock and is not counted a second time. A subclass would have counted 3.

questions.q: Write two delivery strategies, express (₦5,000 fee, i.e. 500000 kobo) and pickup (free), each an object with a feeKobo(order) method, so the program prints 35000 then 30000.
questions.explain: totalNaira delegates the fee to whatever object it is given. New delivery options never require changing it.

questions.q: Finish mixInto(target, ...sources): copy every own key of every source onto target using property descriptors, but throw new Error("clash: " + key) if the key already exists on the target (including inherited keys). The program should print true then clash: describe.
questions.explain: Reflect.ownKeys includes symbol keys, in checks the whole chain, and descriptors keep getters as getters. The clash surfaces when the program starts instead of silently replacing a method.

questions.q: Write a rule factory percentOff(percent) that returns a rule (amount) => … taking percent% off and rounding to a whole kobo with Math.round. With the rules shown, the program should print 903000.
questions.explain: 1,000,000 × 0.84 = 840,000, then × 1.075 = 903,000. The factory returns a function that closes over percent, so each call makes a new rule.

questions.q: Add a static method isTicket(value) to Ticket that uses a brand check on the private field #seat. It must return false (not throw) for null and primitives. The program should print true false false false.
questions.explain: #seat in value throws a TypeError when value is not an object, so check that first. Only objects built by the constructor carry the private field.

questions.q: The Money class keeps its amount in a private field, so JSON.stringify prints {}. Add a toJSON method so the program prints {"price":{"kobo":850000,"currency":"NGN"}}.
questions.explain: JSON.stringify calls toJSON when an object has one and serialises its return value instead. The class decides exactly what leaves it.

questions.q: Write withLimit(gateway, maxKobo), a decorator that returns an object with an async charge(amountKobo, reference). It throws new Error("over limit") for amounts above maxKobo without calling the gateway, and otherwise forwards the call. The program should print paid ORD-1, then over limit, then 1.
questions.explain: The decorator has the same shape as a gateway, so it can wrap any gateway and be wrapped by others. Checking before forwarding means a refused payment never reaches the provider.

questions.q: The product below copies its capability with spread, so left never changes. Replace the spread with a copy that keeps the getter, so the program prints 12 then 2.
questions.explain: Spread stores the getter's current value. Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors plus Object.defineProperties copies the getter function itself, so every read runs it again.
